notes.meaning: Jewish captives sat beside the rivers and canals of Babylon, far from home, and wept. Sitting on the ground was a common sign of deep sorrow and mourning. Remembering Zion and the destroyed temple broke their hearts. Even living in a fertile, wealthy land could not ease their grief over losing the worship of God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that sitting by the waters of Babylon represents believers sitting beside the passing, temporary pleasures of this world and weeping over exile from their true heavenly home.

notes.meaning: The captives hung their musical instruments on the willow trees growing along the waterways. They had no heart to play music or sing cheerful tunes while their city and temple lay in ruins. Instead of smashing their harps, they hung them up in plain view, hoping God would one day let them play again in Jerusalem.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine allegorized the harps as the Scriptures and God's promises, while the willows represent fruitless people living in worldly pleasures upon whom holy words should not be wasted.

notes.meaning: The Babylonian captors added to the prisoners' pain by demanding that they perform happy songs for entertainment. They specifically asked for sacred temple hymns about Zion in order to mock the captives and their God. It was a cruel and ungodly demand that treated holy worship like a circus act.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Fr. Lawrence Farley views this demand as the crowning humiliation for the captives, because it asked them to turn their sacred temple hymns into something like rowdy pagan drinking songs.

notes.meaning: The exiles refused to sing the Lord's sacred hymns for the amusement of idolaters in a foreign country. These songs belonged to the holy worship of God and were never meant for common party music. The captives chose reverent silence rather than treating holy things like cheap entertainment.

The writer swears a personal oath never to forget the holy city of Jerusalem. He calls a curse upon himself, asking that his right hand lose all its skill to play the harp if he ever forgets his true home. Remaining faithful to God and His worship was far more important than pleasing his captors.

The singer also declares that his tongue should stick to the roof of his mouth so he can never speak or sing again if he fails to remember Jerusalem. He places the spiritual joy of God's city and temple above every earthly pleasure. His loyalty to God's kingdom remained his highest priority even in deep exile.

The psalm asks God to hold the nearby nation of Edom accountable for their cruelty when Jerusalem fell. The Edomites were related to Israel through Esau, yet they cheered on the Babylonians and urged them to level Jerusalem to its foundations. Rather than taking revenge into their own hands, the captives left justice entirely to the Lord.

Babylon seemed proud and unbeatable, but the psalmist announces that the city is already doomed to ruin. God would use an avenger, such as the Persian army under Cyrus, to repay Babylon for the savage violence it had brought on others. This destruction would prove that God's righteous justice will always catch up with cruel oppressors.

This harsh picture describes the terrible, complete destruction that ancient warfare would bring upon Babylon. Prophets had foretold that Babylon would reap the exact brutal slaughter it had handed out to other nations, so that its empire would never rise again. The conqueror is called blessed because he serves as God's instrument to execute just judgment against a ruthless world power.

differ.view: Some teachers in this tradition hold that since the cross, believers are called to pray for reconciliation and mercy rather than pronounce judgment against enemies.
Some authors, such as C. S. Lewis, argued that severe curses on enemies reflect sinful human anger rather than words Christians should ever echo.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine allegorized this verse to mean smashing newborn sinful thoughts against the 'rock,' which stands for Christ, before they can grow into full, destructive habits.
